930.bp: An e-commerce site constantly has to estimate a simple-looking question: if this shopper sees this item, will a purchase happen? That number shapes ranking, advertising spend, coupons, and page layout. The trouble is that shoppers are not drawn from one neat crowd. A bargain hunter, a loyal repeat buyer, a person browsing late at night, and a person comparing premium products may follow different decision rules even when the site records them in the same table of features. The paper argues that a single conversion model, with one shared set of internal parameters for every instance, treats these different buying patterns as if they came from one underlying distribution. APPNet serves the practical need to make the predictor adapt by instance group, while avoiding a second problem: humans often do not know in advance which recorded fields should define those groups. The goal is therefore not just conversion prediction, but automatic personalization of the predictor's own settings.
930.wh: The hard part is separating two jobs that look similar in the raw data. Some features should help answer the direct prediction question: given this case, how likely is conversion? Other features should help decide which kind of case this is, so the model can adjust its parameters before making the prediction. Earlier personalized-parameter models group instances and change parameters for each group, but the abstract says they either rely on prior human choices about grouping features or reuse all features for both grouping and prediction. The first route fails because human intuition may miss the actual data distribution. The second route fails during learning because the same feature representation is being pulled toward two goals at once: produce a good conversion score and produce good parameter adjustments. The abstract calls this gradient conflict, meaning the error-reduction signals sent backward through the model can push shared parts in incompatible directions.
930.naive: A smart beginner might train one large conversion predictor on every logged impression, click, item, and user feature, then ask it to learn all buying patterns at once. If that underfits different shopper groups, the next try would be to hand-pick grouping fields, such as user type, product category, or campaign source, and train a personalized-parameter component around those groups. Both attempts are brittle. The universal model averages together cases that may obey different purchase logic. The hand-picked grouping model depends on the designer guessing which fields reveal the real hidden mixture of behaviors. A third naive fix, feeding all features into both the predictor and the parameter generator, creates mixed training signals because the same input parts must serve two different purposes.
930.ap: APPNet's central move is to let the model learn the division of labor among features. It contains Automatic Feature Partitioning, or AFP, and a Parameter Personalized Network, or PPNet. AFP partitions the available features into two parts. One part goes to the main deep neural network, meaning the layered predictor that turns feature values into a conversion score. The other part goes to PPNet, which generates weights used to adjust the main predictor's parameters for the relevant instance group. In the complete abstract available elsewhere in the repo, AFP is described at two granularities: feature-wise partitioning, which splits whole feature fields, and bit-wise partitioning, which splits smaller pieces inside learned feature descriptions. PPNet then applies element-wise multiplication to the conversion model's parameters. In plain terms, it does not replace the predictor; it produces per-group dials that amplify or shrink parts of the predictor before scoring.
930.mech: The mechanism starts with one training instance from the e-commerce log: a set of feature values describing the user, item, context, or other conversion-related facts, plus the observed conversion label used for training. AFP first decides which feature information should be used for the conversion task itself and which should be used as grouping evidence for personalization. In the feature-wise version, the decision is made at the level of whole fields. In the bit-wise version, the decision is finer: individual components of a learned feature description can be routed differently. The prediction-side feature part enters the main conversion DNN, whose job is to compute the buy-or-not likelihood. The grouping-side feature part enters PPNet, whose job is to generate adjustment weights for the DNN parameters. Those adjustment weights are applied by element-wise multiplication, so each selected parameter of the conversion model can be strengthened, weakened, or left mostly unchanged for the current group of instances. During training, the final conversion prediction is compared with the observed outcome, and the error signal updates both the partitioning behavior and the personalized parameter generation. The output is still a conversion prediction, but it is produced by a predictor whose effective settings have been adapted using automatically selected grouping evidence.
930.math: The main mathematical ideas are supervised learning, partitioning, personalized parameters, and error-driven search. Supervised learning means the system sees many past cases where features were followed by conversion or no conversion, then learns a scoring rule that should assign higher purchase chances to cases resembling past converters. Partitioning means splitting one collection into parts according to a criterion. Here the collection is the set of feature information, and the criterion is learned from data rather than written by a person. Personalized parameters mean the predictor does not use exactly the same internal weights for every case; another module produces multipliers that alter those weights for a group of similar instances. Element-wise multiplication is the simple arithmetic move behind that adjustment: each learned setting is paired with a generated factor, and their product becomes the setting used for prediction. The learning process is an optimization loop, meaning it defines wrongness as conversion-prediction error and changes controllable choices to reduce that wrongness. The tradeoff is sharing versus specialization. Share too much and different purchase patterns are averaged together; specialize carelessly and the grouping mechanism fights the predictor or follows accidental noise.
930.dots: This paper sits in the advertising and e-commerce family because it turns partial behavior records into decisions that affect revenue, ranking, and exposure. Its closest neighbor is conversion prediction: like delayed conversion and calibration papers in the repo, it treats purchase likelihood as a probability estimated from repeated cases, not as a certain label known ahead of time. It also connects to recommendation and ranking, because those systems often depend on conversion scores when deciding which item or ad to show. The mathematical link to the broader conference is choosing settings under limits. APPNet chooses which features should guide prediction and which should guide parameter adaptation, then uses feedback to improve that choice. It is also related to personalization papers in recommendation, but with a narrower object: the system is not directly building a user-facing explanation or item list. It is changing the internal conversion predictor so heterogeneous instance groups are not forced through one shared set of parameters.
930.ww: The mechanism should help because it matches the structure described in the abstract: e-commerce instances come from heterogeneous underlying distributions. If two groups of cases obey different conversion rules, one global parameter set must compromise between them. A personalized-parameter model can reduce that compromise by giving different groups different effective settings. APPNet adds a second improvement: it avoids asking humans to decide the grouping evidence in advance. If the data itself shows that certain feature fields or feature components are better for separating behavior types, AFP can route them toward PPNet. At the same time, keeping prediction features and grouping features apart reduces the conflict created when one shared feature representation is trained for two jobs. The predictor can focus on estimating conversion from task-relevant evidence, while PPNet can focus on generating adjustment weights. Element-wise multiplication is also a controlled form of adaptation: it changes existing parameters by scaling them rather than building a completely separate model for every group. That makes personalization more targeted and less wasteful.
930.po: The payoff is a conversion predictor that can adapt its own parameters to different groups of e-commerce instances without relying on hand-written grouping rules. The complete abstract in the repo reports that APPNet outperforms previous parameter-personalized models in offline experiments and that an online production A/B test achieved a 1.09% conversion-rate improvement. Grounded in the abstract, the practical capability is better purchase prediction in a live commerce system where user and item cases are not all governed by the same behavior pattern. The gain is not just a higher score in isolation; it is a more useful probability estimate for downstream ranking, advertising, or promotion decisions.
930.limits: The claim depends on the logged features containing enough signal to separate useful grouping evidence from direct prediction evidence. If the features do not reveal the true behavioral differences, automatic partitioning cannot invent them. The method also assumes that the learned partitions and parameter multipliers remain useful after deployment, where products, users, campaigns, and traffic sources can change. The abstract reports offline experiments and a production A/B test, but it does not show which categories, markets, feature sets, or time periods were covered. It also does not prove that bit-wise partitioning is always worth its extra complexity, or that reducing gradient conflict fully prevents over-specialization to noisy groups.

931.bp: Synthetic data is used when real training data is expensive, private, slow to label, or simply unavailable in enough variety. A language model can help by writing new examples, but the way those examples are requested matters. This paper studies a basic question behind that practice: should the generator first create diverse raw examples and then assign labels, or should it be told the label first and asked to produce examples that fit it? The first order resembles how many real datasets arise: a text, user case, or record exists, and an annotator later decides its class. The second order works backward from the answer. The paper asks whether that reversal changes the usefulness of the resulting data. Using GPT-5 as the generator, it builds synthetic datasets for three machine learning tasks, trains BERT-base and LLaMA-3.2-1B on them, and compares the trained models with human-curated test data.
931.wh: The difficulty is that a label is a very small summary of a richer object. A movie review labeled positive, a question labeled answerable, or a document assigned to a class contains many details that are not fully determined by the label. Real examples include indirect wording, mixed evidence, irrelevant details, borderline cases, and accidental variation. If a language model is prompted with the label first, it may produce examples that make the label too obvious, too clean, or too centered on stereotyped cues. Such data can look valid because every example matches its requested class, but it may not teach a downstream model how real inputs vary. The harder question is not whether the synthetic examples are grammatical or label-consistent. It is whether their distribution, meaning the pattern of examples the training model repeatedly sees, is close enough to human data that learned rules carry over.
931.naive: A smart beginner would generate training data by asking the language model for a fixed number of examples for each label. If the task has three classes, the prompt would name a class and request texts that belong to it. This is attractive because it gives direct control over class balance and avoids a separate labeling step. It fails when the prompt turns the label into a recipe. The generated input may describe the answer rather than contain the subtle evidence from which the answer should be inferred. A classifier trained on that data can learn shortcuts such as label-specific wording or overly tidy examples. When evaluated on human-curated data, those shortcuts no longer match the messier way real examples express the same label.
931.ap: The core idea is to treat data synthesis direction as the object being tested, not as an implementation detail. The paper defines two prompt-controlled routes. In the causal route, the generator first produces diverse raw data, and the data is then annotated for the downstream task. In the anticausal route, label information is placed inside the prompt so the generator produces targeted examples for that label. The study then holds the broad setup fixed: GPT-5 generates the synthetic datasets, two different model families are trained on those datasets, and human-curated benchmarks are used as the outside check. This turns a vague concern into a measurable comparison. If the anticausal route consistently produces worse trained models and its generated data sits farther from human data, then synthesis direction is not cosmetic. It changes what information the training set contains.
931.mech: The mechanism begins with a downstream task that needs labeled examples. The paper constructs two synthetic versions of the task data. For the causal version, the prompt asks the language model to create raw examples without first forcing a target label into the generation request. Those examples are then annotated for the task, so the label is attached after the example exists. For the anticausal version, the prompt includes label information up front, and the language model is asked to produce examples aimed at that label. The output of each route is a labeled synthetic dataset. Next, the authors train two kinds of downstream models on these datasets: BERT-base and LLaMA-3.2-1B. This matters because a weakness that appears across both a smaller encoder-style text model and a small language model is less likely to be a quirk of one architecture. After training, the models are evaluated against human-curated benchmarks rather than only against synthetic test material. Finally, the paper performs distributional analysis, which means comparing the overall pattern of generated data with the pattern of human data. The reported result is consistent across three tasks: models trained on anticausal synthetic data lose more accuracy, and anticausal datasets deviate farther from human data.
931.math: The main mathematical idea is causal direction. In everyday terms, causal direction asks which thing is treated as coming first in the story of how data is made. In ordinary labeled data, the example usually carries evidence, and the label summarizes one property of that example. Anticausal prompting reverses that order by starting with the summary and asking for an example that fits it. The second idea is probability over data, which here means the mix of cases a learner is likely to see. A training set is not just a list; it is a repeated source of evidence. If one source overproduces clean label-signaling cases and underproduces ambiguous or rare human cases, a model trained on it will estimate the wrong rules. The third idea is generalization, meaning reuse of a learned pattern on new examples. The study checks generalization by training on synthetic data and testing on human-curated benchmarks. Distributional comparison is the bridge between these ideas: it asks whether two piles of examples have similar shapes, not merely whether each individual example is plausible. The tradeoff is controllability versus realism. Label-conditioned generation gives easy control over what classes appear, but that control can erase natural variation. Causal generation gives up some directness in exchange for examples whose labels arise after richer content is present.
931.dots: This paper belongs to the conference thread about language models as data producers. It connects to synthetic-data papers that ask when artificial examples can stand in for costly or sensitive real examples, but its special focus is the direction of construction. It also sits near causal-inference work because the central warning is about confusing a surface association with the process that produced it. The label and the text are related, but building text backward from the label is not the same as observing text and then labeling it. The paper also connects to recommendation, retrieval, and classification work where training data quietly defines what the model thinks the world looks like. If the generated pile is too tidy, every later ranking or prediction system inherits that narrow view. Compared with papers that design new generators, this one is more diagnostic: it asks which generation habit makes downstream learning less trustworthy.
931.ww: The causal route should work better because it preserves more of the information that exists before a label is assigned. A real annotator often sees a full example first: the wording, context, irrelevant pieces, mixed signals, and then the class. That means the label is only one consequence of a richer object. When synthetic generation follows that order, the model being trained is exposed to examples where the answer must be inferred from several cues. In the anticausal route, the label is available before the text is made, so the language model can satisfy the prompt by writing examples that strongly display the requested class. That creates training data with less need for inference. The downstream model then practices an easier problem than the one it faces on human data. The empirical pattern in the abstract supports this intuition: anticausal training causes larger accuracy drops for both BERT and LLaMA model families, and the distributional analysis says those datasets are farther from human data. The reason is not magic in the causal prompt; it is that generation order changes what variety survives into the training signal.
931.po: The payoff is practical guidance for anyone using language models to create training data. The paper shows that prompt direction can materially affect downstream utility, not just surface style. In the reported experiments, models trained on anticausal synthetic data suffer larger accuracy drops across all three tasks and both model families, with declines of 13.7 percent to 59.1 percent for BERT and 4.9 percent to 54.3 percent for LLaMA. The distributional analysis also finds anticausal synthetic datasets farther from human data. The useful lesson is simple: when synthetic examples are meant to teach a model about real inputs, generate richer inputs first and label them afterward when possible.
931.limits: The abstract supports a clear empirical warning, but it does not identify every task, dataset, labeling procedure, or distributional measure used in the study. The conclusion depends on the prompting strategies being fair representatives of causal and anticausal synthesis. Different prompts, stronger post-filtering, human review, or task-specific constraints might reduce the anticausal gap. The work also uses GPT-5 as the generator, so the exact pattern may differ with another model. Human-curated benchmarks are a strong outside check, but they only represent the tested domains. The paper shows that synthesis direction matters in the examined settings; it does not prove that label-conditioned generation is always bad or that causal prompting alone guarantees high-quality synthetic data.

932.bp: Automated fact-checking is useful only if the system can keep a claim, the outside evidence, and its own prior belief separate. The ordinary task is simple to state: someone gives a claim, the system gathers evidence, and it decides whether the evidence supports or refutes the claim. Large language models complicate that task because they do not arrive empty-handed. They already contain facts and false facts learned during training. KnowFC is aimed at the moment when a retrieved passage says one thing while the model's stored belief says another. In that moment, a fluent model can sound certain while following the wrong source. The paper treats fact-checking as a conflict-management problem, not just a search problem. Its goal is to decide when the model should rely on what it already knows, when it should retrieve more evidence, and how to stop wrong internal knowledge from overpowering external evidence.
932.wh: The difficulty is that confidence and correctness are different things. A language model can be confident because a pattern appeared often during training, because a claim sounds familiar, or because its answer style rewards decisiveness. None of that proves the claim is true. External evidence is also imperfect: it may be incomplete, loosely related, or inconsistent with what the model has memorized. A simple fact-checking pipeline usually retrieves evidence and asks the model to judge the claim using that evidence. KnowFC argues that this overlooks a hidden fight inside the model. If the model already believes a wrong answer, the retrieved evidence may not correct it. The model may explain away the evidence, ignore it, or blend it with its prior belief. The hard part is therefore not only finding documents. It is measuring the model's knowledge boundary and preventing false internal certainty from steering the final verification.
932.naive: A smart beginner would build a fact-checker by taking a claim, retrieving several relevant passages, and prompting a language model to decide whether the claim is true. If the retrieved evidence looks strong, the beginner would expect the model to follow it. This fails when the model brings a competing memory into the decision. Suppose the evidence contradicts what the model thinks it knows. The prompt may show the evidence, but the model can still lean on its old belief, especially when it is overconfident. Another naive fix is to always retrieve more evidence. That wastes effort when the model already knows enough and still may not help when the model refuses to yield to evidence. More documents do not solve the problem if the judge is biased toward its own memory.
932.ap: KnowFC's central move is to split the model's knowledge into two practical regions: things it seems to know reliably and things it does not know or may only think it knows. The system then uses that split to decide how much outside evidence to retrieve. This is adaptive retrieval: evidence gathering changes according to the model's estimated knowledge boundary instead of being the same for every claim. To learn this boundary, the paper trains the model with reinforcement learning, meaning the model tries actions and receives feedback that rewards better behavior. The reward is inspired by the Dunning-Kruger effect: the system should penalize confident ignorance and encourage better calibration between confidence and actual correctness. After evidence is retrieved, KnowFC builds reasoning graphs from that evidence and uses causal mediation analysis to reduce interference from the model's internal knowledge during verification.
932.mech: The input is a claim that needs verification by a language-model-based fact-checking system. First, KnowFC asks the model to expose a useful signal about whether the claim falls inside or outside its knowledge boundary. The paper describes this as confidence calibration: the model's confidence is trained to be informative rather than merely forceful. During training, reinforcement learning supplies feedback so that the model is rewarded when its confidence better matches what it can actually verify and punished when it acts certain while being wrong. That calibrated signal controls retrieval. For claims the model does not know well, the system should retrieve external evidence; for claims it can handle reliably, it can avoid unnecessary retrieval and save effort. Next, the retrieved evidence is organized into reasoning graphs. In plain terms, the system turns pieces of evidence and their relationships into a connected structure so the verification step can follow how one piece supports, contradicts, or depends on another. Finally, KnowFC applies causal intervention using causal mediation analysis. This step treats internal knowledge as a possible hidden influence on the answer and tries to reduce that influence, so the final judgment is driven more by the evidence graph than by the model's pre-existing belief. The output is a fact-checking decision made after adaptive evidence retrieval and debiased verification.
932.math: Three mathematical ideas carry the paper. The first is calibrated confidence. Calibration means that a confidence score should behave like a trustworthy warning label: when the model says it is highly sure, it should usually be right, and when it is unsure, the system should know to seek help. The second idea is reinforcement learning, explained here as learning by trying a decision policy and receiving rewards for decisions that lead to better fact-checking behavior. The important part is not a game-like metaphor; it is that KnowFC can reward the model for recognizing its own boundary rather than only for producing an answer. The Dunning-Kruger-inspired reward targets the specific mistake of confident ignorance. The third idea is causal mediation analysis. Causal reasoning asks what would change if one influence were changed while competing influences were separated. Mediation analysis studies whether an intermediate factor carries an effect from one source to an outcome. Here, the unwanted source is internal model knowledge, the outcome is the verification answer, and the paper tries to weaken the path by which internal belief interferes with evidence-based reasoning. The reasoning graph adds a graph idea: evidence pieces become connected objects, and links describe how support or contradiction can travel among them.
932.dots: This paper connects several recurring conference pressures. It belongs to LLM fact-checking because the practical object is a claim judged by a language model using evidence. It also sits near retrieval work, where the central problem is choosing which outside information should be brought into a small decision context. Unlike generic retrieval, KnowFC makes retrieval depend on the model's estimated self-knowledge. It connects to graph reasoning because retrieved evidence is not treated as a loose pile; it is organized so relationships among evidence pieces can guide verification. It also connects to causal inference because the paper treats internal knowledge as an interfering influence whose effect on the answer must be separated from the effect of external evidence. Neighboring misinformation and trust papers ask similar questions in different forms: how to prevent fluent systems from making unsupported claims, how to retrieve evidence that matters for verification, and how to keep the final judgment grounded rather than merely plausible.
932.ww: The approach should work better than the naive pipeline because it addresses the failure before and after retrieval. Before retrieval, the system asks whether the model is in a region where its own knowledge can be trusted. That prevents two opposite errors: wasting retrieval on easy known claims and skipping retrieval on claims where the model is merely overconfident. The reward design matters because a model that learns only to answer may become more polished without becoming more honest about uncertainty. By rewarding confidence that matches actual correctness, KnowFC tries to make uncertainty useful for action. After retrieval, the evidence graph gives the verifier structure. Instead of reading evidence as disconnected snippets, the system can reason over how pieces relate. The causal mediation step then attacks a deeper bias: even with good evidence, the model's prior belief can still leak into the answer. Reducing that path makes the final decision more evidence-led. The intuitive cause of improvement is separation: separate known from unknown, evidence from memory, and support relationships from loose text.
932.po: The payoff is a fact-checking system that can navigate knowledge conflicts rather than pretending they do not exist. The abstract claims KnowFC improves correctness and efficiency by adaptively using what the model knows and does not know. Correctness should improve because overconfident wrong internal knowledge is less able to dominate the answer. Efficiency should improve because retrieval is not automatic for every claim; it is guided by estimated need. The system also buys a more reliable verification process by organizing evidence into reasoning graphs and applying a debiasing step aimed at internal-knowledge interference. The visible abstract says experimental results exist, but it is truncated before giving the concrete datasets, numbers, or comparisons.
932.limits: Several assumptions have to hold. Confidence calibration must actually reveal the model's knowledge boundary; if the confidence signal is itself unreliable, adaptive retrieval will make poor choices. The retrieval system must be able to find evidence that is relevant and trustworthy when the model needs help. The reasoning graph must represent useful support and contradiction relationships rather than adding structure that only looks orderly. The causal mediation step assumes internal knowledge interference can be identified well enough to reduce it without removing useful background knowledge. The abstract does not prove generality across domains, languages, evidence quality, claim types, or adversarial misinformation. Because the input abstract is truncated, the reported experimental strength cannot be assessed here.

933.bp: The ordinary problem is this: many organizations store facts as a connected map. A drug connects to a disease, a customer connects to purchases, a company connects to owners, and a person connects to attributes such as age, location, or role. The paper asks a harder question than filling or searching that map. It asks what would change if one entity received a treatment, exposure, policy, or condition, when the evidence lives inside an incomplete knowledge graph. That matters because a decision maker may want to know whether a medical intervention, recommendation, subsidy, warning, or policy actually changes an outcome rather than merely appearing beside it. BaLu serves settings where the graph gives useful relational context, but the graph is not a clean table. Some attributes are missing because the map only records known facts, and entities can influence one another through links. The paper tries to estimate cause-and-effect relationships without pretending the graph is complete or that each entity is isolated.
933.wh: The difficulty comes from two breaks in the simple causal story. First, a knowledge graph usually follows an open-world assumption: if a fact is absent, it does not mean the fact is false. It may simply not have been observed or added. For causal inference, missing attributes are dangerous because attributes often explain both who receives treatment and what outcome follows. If those attributes are absent, the comparison between treated and untreated entities can be unfair. Second, graph entities are linked. One entity's treatment or state can affect another entity's outcome through relational dependency. The abstract calls this interference. A usual treatment-effect estimate wants units to be separate, like sealed boxes. Knowledge graphs are closer to a city map, where changing one place can affect nearby places. Existing methods that assume full observation or ignore inter-unit dependence can therefore produce biased or unreliable effect estimates, even if their prediction machinery looks strong.
933.naive: A smart beginner would turn the knowledge graph into a table, keep the attributes that are present, ignore blanks, and estimate treatment effects as if each entity were independent. A slightly more careful beginner might first fill missing attributes with a separate imputation method, then run a standard causal model. Both versions fail for the same reason: they split one coupled problem into pieces that actually depend on each other. Filling attributes without using the causal task may create plausible but causally unhelpful values. Estimating effects without modeling graph links misses spillover from related entities. The result can compare entities that only look similar because important attributes were missing, or treat a neighbor's influence as if it were the entity's own treatment effect.
933.ap: The core idea of BaLu is to learn the missing-attribute problem and the treatment-effect problem together on the same graph. Instead of treating absent attributes as a preprocessing nuisance, BaLu reformulates attribute imputation as edge prediction: the system asks whether an entity should be connected to a particular attribute. Instead of treating causal estimation as a flat table problem, it reformulates treatment-effect estimation as node prediction that is aware of interference: each entity's outcome estimate can depend on messages arriving through graph relations. Graph neural networks supply the machinery for this joint learning. In plain terms, every entity updates its description by listening to nearby entities, attributes, and relations. That updated description is then used both to infer missing attribute links and to estimate treatment effects. The point is that the same relational structure that makes the graph hard is also evidence that can help repair the missing facts and model spillover.
933.mech: The input is a knowledge graph: entities, relations between entities, observed attributes, treatment information, and outcomes or labels needed for effect estimation. BaLu first treats observed entity-attribute facts as edges in the graph. When an attribute is missing, the model does not simply mark it as false. It scores possible entity-attribute edges and predicts which missing connections are likely, using both attribute similarity and the surrounding relational structure. At the same time, the model builds a learned description for each entity through graph neural network message passing. Message passing means that an entity repeatedly combines its own available information with transformed information from linked neighbors. The transformation matters because different relations can carry different kinds of evidence: a shared category, ownership link, biological relation, or social relation should not all mean the same thing. The imputation part supplies more complete attribute evidence, while the node-prediction part estimates treatment effects with awareness that linked entities are not independent. These two tasks are interconnected during training, so better attribute recovery can improve causal estimates, and the causal-estimation need can shape which recovered attributes matter. The output is a set of inferred attributes and interference-aware effect estimates for graph entities. The abstract reports experiments on four datasets comparing BaLu with baselines, including baselines strengthened with imputation techniques.
933.math: The main mathematical ideas are graph-based evidence movement, missing-value estimation, probability-like scoring, and causal comparison. A graph is a set of places and roads: entities and attributes are places, and relations or attribute memberships are roads. The assumption is not that every neighbor is the same, but that a link gives controlled permission for evidence to travel. Attribute imputation is a prediction problem over missing edges. The model scores whether an entity and an attribute should be connected, using patterns seen elsewhere in the graph. This uses similarity in an everyday sense: entities with related positions, neighbors, or attributes give clues about one another, while the score compresses many differences into a single judgment. Treatment-effect estimation is a causal comparison: what outcome would be expected with treatment versus without treatment? Because only one of those worlds is observed for each entity, the model must build a fair comparison from repeated cases and graph context. Interference adds network math to causality: the outcome for one node may change when neighboring nodes carry treatment or outcome signals. The tradeoff is local independence versus relational realism. Ignoring links makes the math simpler but false for connected graphs; trusting links too much can spread wrong or missing information into the causal estimate.
933.dots: Within the repo's map, this paper sits directly between the causal-inference family and the knowledge-graph family. The causal-inference family asks how to repair a broken comparison before using data to guide action. BaLu's broken comparison comes from missing attributes and interference: treated and untreated entities may differ in facts the graph failed to record, and neighbors may leak influence across units. The knowledge-graph family asks how connected facts should be completed, followed, and trusted. BaLu uses that same connected structure not only to answer questions or complete links, but to estimate effects. It is also a sibling of gid 909, which handles network interference by separating hidden causal factors for each unit. The difference is the surface object: gid 909 focuses on networked observational data and hidden factor roles, while BaLu focuses on knowledge graphs where missing entity-attribute edges are part of the causal problem. It also connects to graph learning papers that use message passing, and to imputation papers that treat missing data as an active modeling problem rather than a blank cell to ignore.
933.ww: BaLu should work better than the naive approach because it aligns the repair step with the causal task. If attributes are missing under an open-world assumption, absence is ambiguous. A separate imputation method may fill blanks by general plausibility, but causal inference needs a specific kind of repair: attributes that help make treatment and outcome comparisons fair. Joint learning gives the model a way to learn attribute completion and effect estimation from the same relational evidence. Graph message passing helps because a knowledge graph's links are not decoration; they encode constraints. If several related entities share attributes or outcomes, that pattern can make a missing entity-attribute edge more believable. The same neighbor evidence can also warn the model that one entity's outcome may partly reflect another entity's treatment or state. This is better than assuming independence because interference is explicitly represented as information moving through links. It is better than using only observed attributes because it treats missing facts as uncertain recoverable evidence. The gain depends on the graph links carrying real similarity or influence rather than accidental association.
933.po: The payoff is a causal-estimation pipeline built for incomplete, relational knowledge graphs instead of clean standalone tables. The abstract says BaLu addresses missing attributes through edge prediction and interference through graph-based representation learning, then combines both in an end-to-end solution. It reports consistent gains over existing baselines on four benchmark datasets, including baselines enhanced with strong imputation techniques. Grounded in the abstract, the practical capability is not merely filling more graph facts. It is estimating treatment effects in a setting where missing attributes and neighbor dependence would otherwise bias the answer. That makes the method relevant for graph-backed decision systems that need action guidance, not only association scores.
933.limits: The claims depend on the knowledge graph being informative enough for both tasks. If missing attributes are missing in a way the graph cannot reveal, edge prediction may confidently fill the wrong facts. If graph links represent administrative grouping, noisy extraction, or stale records rather than real similarity or influence, message passing can spread bias. The treatment-effect estimates also require causal assumptions that the abstract cannot fully state: what counts as treatment, outcome, interference, and sufficient adjustment must be credible. The abstract is truncated, so details about datasets, effect definitions, and evaluation design are not visible here. Reported benchmark gains do not by themselves prove reliability in deployed graphs with adversarial edges, changing facts, rare entities, or unmeasured causes.

934.bp: Phishing detection starts from a very ordinary danger: a user is shown a web domain that looks close enough to a bank, postal service, or other trusted service that the user may type in credentials or personal details. The system being protected is not just a browser page. It is the chain of trust between a person, a web address, and the real organization the address appears to represent. U-Proof serves that moment of judgment. It asks whether modern generative language models, together with more traditional machine learning models, can help decide when a website is trying to impersonate a legitimate service. The paper matters because online services keep expanding, which gives attackers more chances to create convincing domains and pages. It also matters because the tool is not only a detector. The abstract says it includes explanations meant to improve user awareness of phishing tactics, so the practical goal is both blocking risky websites and teaching people what made them risky.
934.wh: The hard part is that phishing lives in small, shifting differences. A bad domain may borrow a trusted name, use a nearly believable spelling, copy the feel of a bank or postal page, or appear only during an active campaign. A detector must separate a dangerous imitation from a legitimate address without treating every unfamiliar domain as malicious. That tension is visible in the paper's data choice: it uses active phishing websites from September 2024 and also URLs from banks and postal services. Those examples stand for two sides that can look uncomfortably close. The task is also hard because different model families may notice different clues. A traditional model may depend on counted features or learned patterns from past URLs. A large language model may reason over text-like clues and produce an explanation, but it can also be overconfident. The paper therefore compares model architectures instead of assuming one style of model is enough.
934.naive: A smart beginner might start with a blacklist: keep a table of known phishing domains and block exact matches. That fails when attackers create new domains faster than the list is updated, or slightly change names to dodge exact matching. The next beginner move would be a hand-written rule such as flag domains that contain bank-like words, odd punctuation, or strange endings. That catches some obvious attacks but also risks flagging legitimate bank or postal URLs, especially if the service uses regional domains or campaign-specific pages. A third simple move is to ask one powerful language model for a yes-or-no judgment. The abstract's comparison agenda suggests why that is insufficient: the important question is not whether one model sounds plausible, but which model type reliably separates active phishing from legitimate service URLs.
934.ap: The core idea of U-Proof is to treat phishing detection as both a model-comparison problem and a user-facing warning problem. Instead of building only one classifier, the tool brings together large language models and traditional machine learning models, then evaluates their ability to identify phishing websites on a mix of public and custom datasets. Mechanically, this means the paper asks a controlled question: when the same kind of web-domain evidence is shown to different architectures, which ones are better at recognizing the phishing pattern? The abstract does not describe every feature, prompt, or algorithm, so the safe inference is limited to the stated comparison between generative models and several ML models. The additional move is explanatory: U-Proof includes reasons or cues behind a detection so a user can learn what tactic was used. That changes the detector from a silent gate into a tool for awareness.
934.mech: The mechanism begins with examples of websites and URLs. Some examples come from public datasets, some from custom datasets, and the abstract names two important custom-looking sources: active phishing websites from September 2024 and URLs from banks and postal services. Each example is fed into detection models. The traditional machine learning side likely treats the web-domain evidence as measurable features, but the abstract does not specify which features, so the reliable description is broader: those models transform each site or URL into signals that can be scored as phishing or legitimate. The language-model side treats the evidence as material it can interpret and classify, comparing suspicious web-domain clues against what it has learned about how legitimate and deceptive web pages tend to be described or structured. The evaluation then compares model architectures by their ability to identify phishing websites. The output is not only a label. U-Proof also produces explanations, so after a website is judged risky, the tool can point to phishing tactics that made the decision understandable. The full loop is therefore: collect current and reference domains, pass them through several model families, compare their detection behavior, and surface both a warning and an explanation to support user protection.
934.math: The central mathematical idea is classification, which means sorting cases into categories by learning which observable clues usually separate one category from another. Here the categories are phishing website and non-phishing service URL. A traditional model does this by converting a domain or site into numbers, then learning a boundary: cases on one side are treated as suspicious, cases on the other side as legitimate. The useful question is what differences should count. A spelling change, a service name, a domain ending, or page wording may matter, but any single clue can mislead. Probability is also present in the background: the system must act under uncertainty, because a website can look partly suspicious and partly normal. A model score is a way of saying how strongly the available evidence points toward phishing. The language-model comparison adds another mathematical object: a model trained on large amounts of text can use patterns in language and web descriptions to judge whether a domain or page resembles known deceptive behavior. The tradeoff is accuracy versus explainability and recency. A detector needs learned pattern recognition, but phishing changes quickly, so the September 2024 active sites are important because they test whether learned clues still match current attacks.
934.dots: This paper sits near several recurring conference ideas even though its surface topic is cyber safety. It connects to trust and misinformation work because both ask whether a digital object should be believed when surface appearance is cheap to fake. A phishing domain is like a false claim with a clickable address: it borrows trust from a known institution and asks the user to act before checking evidence. It also connects to retrieval and ranking because a deployed detector may have to inspect many candidate URLs and prioritize which ones deserve warnings. The comparison between language models and traditional models connects to the broader question of when generative models are useful evaluators rather than just text producers. Finally, it belongs near privacy and security work because the protected object is user information. The neighboring decentralized phishing paper in the repo studies how attackers exploit web infrastructure such as IPFS gateways; U-Proof focuses instead on classifying web domains and explaining phishing tactics to users.
934.ww: The approach can work better than the naive options because it does not rely on one brittle clue. A blacklist only remembers what has already been seen. A hand-written rule only catches what its designer anticipated. U-Proof's comparison of multiple model architectures creates a way to ask which kind of learned pattern recognition is actually useful for current phishing websites and legitimate bank or postal URLs. Traditional models may be good at stable, measurable signs that repeat across many examples. Large language models may be useful when the clue is more semantic: the wording, organization name, or apparent service context may need interpretation rather than exact matching. The explanation component helps for a different reason. Users are not just protected by a hidden label; they can see why the site looked suspicious, which may make the warning more actionable and may teach them to notice similar tactics later. The method works if the datasets contain enough realistic contrast between active phishing sites and legitimate service URLs for these model differences to become visible.
934.po: The payoff is a phishing-detection tool, U-Proof, that evaluates modern language models alongside several traditional machine learning models instead of assuming a single best detector. Grounded in the abstract, the concrete capability is identifying phishing websites using a combination of public and custom datasets, including active September 2024 phishing websites and URLs from banks and postal services. The user-facing payoff is also educational: explanations can show which phishing tactics triggered concern. That matters because phishing defense is partly a speed problem and partly a human judgment problem. A better warning is useful, but a warning that teaches the pattern can reduce later risk as well.
934.limits: The abstract does not prove that U-Proof will catch future phishing campaigns, only that the paper evaluates models on the stated datasets. Active sites from September 2024 make the evaluation more realistic, but phishing tactics change, and attackers may adapt once they know which clues detectors use. The abstract also does not specify the features, prompts, model names, error rates, or deployment setting, so claims about the exact mechanism must stay general. The tool assumes that public and custom datasets represent the difference between phishing and legitimate bank or postal URLs well enough. Explanations help awareness only if they are faithful to the model's actual evidence and understandable to users under pressure.

935.bp: A recommendation system is often asked to make a small prediction at the exact moment a person is choosing what to watch, read, buy, or click next. The useful evidence is not only the bag of things the person liked before. Order matters. A user who looked at phones, then cases, then chargers is in a different state from someone who looked at chargers months ago and phones today. This paper serves that setting: sequential recommendation, where the system tries to extend a user's recent behavior into a next-item suggestion. The abstract says recent diffusion models have been promising here. In plain terms, a diffusion model starts from a noisy candidate and repeatedly cleans it toward something that fits learned behavior. The paper's claim is that this cleaning process should not be guided by one compressed user summary alone. It should also keep explicit user-item interactions and sequential patterns visible while the recommendation is formed.
935.wh: The hard part is that user behavior has several kinds of evidence at once. Some evidence is implicit: a learned summary of taste, habit, and context that is not written as a simple rule. Some evidence is explicit: the actual interactions, item choices, and observed order in the sequence. Existing implicit conditional diffusion approaches, according to the abstract, compress user behaviors into a single representation during the forward diffusion process. That can work when the compressed summary keeps the important signal, but it can erase why the next action is likely. If the summary forgets the exact order, recent context, or direct user-item links, the model may recommend something generally similar but wrong for the current moment. The opposite mistake is also possible: using explicit patterns too directly can follow noise, repeated accidents, or irrelevant behaviors. The tension is to combine both signals dynamically without letting either flatten or contaminate the other.
935.naive: A smart beginner might summarize each user's history into one vector-like profile, meaning one compact list of numbers that stands in for the person's interests, and then ask a model to produce the next recommendation from that profile. This is attractive because it turns a messy sequence into a tidy input. The failure is that tidiness can remove the very evidence that makes sequential recommendation different from ordinary recommendation. The same items in a different order can imply a different intent. A one-piece summary may also blur direct user-item interactions with broader preference patterns. If the user clicked an item for a temporary reason, the model may treat it as stable taste; if the user has a clear recent pattern, the model may wash it out.
935.ap: The paper's central move is to give the diffusion process two kinds of guidance instead of one. It proposes Dual Conditional Diffusion Models for Sequential Recommendation, called DCRec, and a Dual Conditional Diffusion Transformer, called DCDT. The key idea is not simply to add more features. It is to place dual conditions into both directions of the diffusion procedure: the forward stage, where the data is gradually noised or compressed for learning, and the reverse stage, where the model cleans noise away to form a recommendation. One condition carries implicit information, the learned behavioral pattern that can capture hidden preference. The other carries explicit information, such as user-item interactions and sequential patterns that directly show what happened. The transformer component dynamically integrates these signals across diffusion stages, so the model can use context while reducing the influence of irrelevant behavior.
935.mech: The mechanism starts with a user's behavior sequence: observed interactions between a user and items, arranged in time. From this, the model has to prepare two forms of condition. The implicit condition is a learned behavioral description, a compressed signal that tries to capture the user's underlying preference and context. The explicit condition keeps more direct evidence, such as which items were interacted with and what sequential pattern those interactions form. During the forward diffusion process, the model does not let behavior collapse into only one undifferentiated summary. It embeds both conditions, so the noisy version of the sequence still carries separate guidance about broad preference and concrete interaction structure. During the reverse diffusion process, the model begins from a noisier candidate state and repeatedly cleans it. At each stage, the Dual Conditional Diffusion Transformer combines the two conditions. It can attend, in the everyday sense of assigning more weight, to parts of the user's history that are useful for the current recommendation and downplay patterns that look irrelevant. The score being improved is whether the cleaned candidate fits the observed user sequence and the explicit interaction evidence. The output is a recommendation signal for the next item, shaped by both hidden preference and observed sequential context.
935.math: The main mathematical idea is denoising as controlled reconstruction. Instead of choosing an item with one direct rule, a diffusion model learns how real behavior looks after it has been gradually corrupted by noise, then learns the reverse move: remove the corruption step by step. This fits sequential recommendation because the next choice is uncertain and noisy. User histories contain stable taste, short-term intent, and accidental clicks mixed together. A second idea is conditioning, which means making a prediction while holding some evidence in view. Here there are two conditions. The implicit condition is a learned summary of behavior; the explicit condition is the observed interaction and sequence evidence. The tradeoff is compression versus detail. Compression helps the model reuse patterns across many users, but loses timing and context. Detail preserves concrete evidence, but can carry noise. The transformer part supplies a learned weighting mechanism: it decides which parts of the sequence and which condition matter more at each stage. That is a mathematical scoring problem, because the model must assign relative importance rather than follow a fixed rule. The underlying bet is that better recommendations come from repeatedly balancing broad preference against direct sequential evidence.
935.dots: This paper sits at the crossing of three recurring conference ideas. One is recommendation as ranking under uncertainty: from a large pile of items, the system must put likely next choices near the top even though it sees only partial behavior. A second is sequence modeling: the order of observations carries meaning, so the model must treat time as evidence rather than as decoration. A third is generative diffusion, where a system constructs a plausible answer by gradually cleaning a noisy candidate. The neighboring papers in this part of the repo include other recommendation and diffusion work, including bundle recommendation and sequential recommendation methods that also worry about sparse data, hard negatives, or drift away from user preference. The shared deeper problem is choosing a small useful set from many possibilities while the evidence is incomplete, noisy, and time dependent.
935.ww: The approach should work better than the one-summary version when the two evidence types correct each other's weaknesses. The implicit condition can notice broad regularities: users with similar histories often move toward similar items, and some item transitions repeat across many people. But broad regularity alone can miss the user's current path. The explicit condition anchors the process to actual interactions and sequence patterns, so the reverse diffusion steps do not clean the candidate toward a generic preference profile. At the same time, explicit behavior alone can overreact to accidental clicks or irrelevant old actions. The learned diffusion process can treat noisy or weak patterns as things to be cleaned away rather than copied. Putting both conditions into both forward and reverse stages matters because the model learns the same distinction while corrupting examples and while rebuilding them. The transformer helps because the useful balance is not fixed: one user may need recent context, another may need stable taste, and a third may need direct item-to-item transition evidence.
935.po: The payoff is a recommendation model that can preserve more of the information that sequential recommendation depends on. According to the abstract, DCRec uses both implicit behavioral information and explicit user-item or sequential information, and DCDT integrates these signals throughout the diffusion stages. That buys a more precise next-item prediction process: the model is not limited to a single compressed profile, and it is not forced to rely only on raw observed clicks. The abstract reports extensive experiments on public datasets and says the method significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods. Grounded in the stated contribution, the practical capability is cleaner next-step recommendation when order and context matter.
935.limits: The abstract leaves several assumptions unproved. The method depends on the dual conditions actually separating useful hidden preference from useful explicit interaction evidence; if both contain the same bias or noise, combining them may reinforce the wrong signal. It also assumes the transformer can learn when to downplay irrelevant behavior without direct human labels for relevance. Public benchmark results show comparative performance, but they do not by themselves prove reliability in live systems with changing catalogs, shifting user intent, feedback loops, or privacy constraints. The abstract also does not specify cost. Diffusion-style repeated cleaning can be heavier than simpler recommenders, so speed and deployment tradeoffs matter.

936.bp: The ordinary problem behind this workshop is choice under scientific uncertainty. Many researchers now build tools that try to answer cause questions: which variables drive an outcome, what would change if an action changed, or which hidden relation explains an observed pattern. A hospital, platform, policy team, or scientist cannot use every causal model at once; someone must choose a method, a dataset, a computing setup, and a way to judge whether the answer is trustworthy. The abstract says that choice is currently hard because causal discovery and causal inference models behave differently across data and hardware or software platforms. CausalBench is therefore not a paper about one new causal method. It is a community effort to make comparison itself more disciplined, by organizing benchmarking data, algorithms, models, and metrics so users can select a setup that fits their specific problem rather than trusting scattered claims.
936.wh: Causal learning is hard to compare because the thing being judged is not just prediction accuracy. A model may find patterns that appear together, but causal work asks a stricter question: what would change if one part of the world were changed while look-alike explanations were held apart? Different tasks emphasize different failures. Causal discovery asks for the shape of the cause map, while causal inference asks for the size or direction of an effect. A method that works on one kind of data may fail on another because missing variables, noisy measurements, sample size, or the computing environment change the apparent evidence. The abstract also points to reproducibility: if the same model is trained on different data or different hardware and software platforms, its reported performance can vary. Without a public, configurable benchmark collection, users cannot tell whether a method is broadly reliable or merely favored by one test setting.
936.naive: A smart beginner would gather a few popular causal methods, run each one on a convenient dataset, record a score, and rank the methods from best to worst. That feels reasonable because many machine learning tasks are compared this way. It fails here because the dataset, task definition, platform, and metric can secretly decide the winner. A method may look strong because the data match its assumptions, because the evaluation ignores a failure mode, or because another team used a different setup. The result is not a fair market of ideas; it is a set of partial demonstrations that are difficult for users to translate into their own problem instance.
936.ap: The central move is to treat benchmarking as an object of research rather than as housekeeping after the real work. The workshop proposes a concerted effort: survey the fast-growing causal learning field, categorize existing benchmarking efforts into technically meaningful groups, find urgent gaps, and invite work on data, algorithms, models, and metrics. In concrete terms, it asks the community to agree on what must be compared and how the comparison should be configured. That matters because causal learning has several different jobs. Some systems try to discover which variables point to which others. Some estimate what a treatment, action, or exposure changes. Some need fairness and bias awareness because wrong comparisons can mislead users. CausalBench's idea is that scientific collaboration around common test beds can make method design and method selection more objective.
936.mech: The mechanism begins with the current landscape: many causal discovery and causal inference models, many datasets, many evaluation habits, and many computing setups. The workshop first calls for a survey of that landscape, because comparison cannot be repaired until the community knows which kinds of tasks already have support and which do not. Next, it groups existing benchmarking efforts by technical meaning rather than by name alone. A group might be defined by the causal task being tested, the kind of data used, the algorithm family being compared, or the metric used to judge success. Then the effort looks for holes: tasks without public data, metrics that do not capture bias, algorithms that cannot be compared under the same conditions, or setups that are not configurable enough for real users. The output is not a single score. It is a shared testing environment and research agenda where a user can ask: for my causal problem, which benchmark setting resembles my data, which metrics measure the error I care about, and which model behaves reliably across the available configurations? The workshop format is part of the mechanism too, because it collects papers and discussion around datasets, algorithms, models, and metrics instead of letting each team define comparison in isolation.
936.math: The main mathematical idea is controlled comparison. In ordinary language, a benchmark should make competing methods face the same question under the same rules, so a difference in score is more likely to reflect the method and less likely to reflect an accident of setup. For causal learning, the comparison has two layers. The first layer is causal reasoning itself: separate a real driver from a pattern that merely travels with it. The second layer is meta-causal in spirit: separate a real method advantage from a testing artifact. A metric is a rule for turning many successes and mistakes into a number, but the number is useful only if it measures the right mistake. For causal discovery, the mistake may be drawing a wrong arrow, missing an arrow, or reversing direction. For causal inference, the mistake may be estimating the wrong change under an action. Configurability is also mathematical because it changes the test conditions in a controlled way: data type, model class, and computing platform can be varied while other parts are held steady. The tradeoff is breadth versus precision. A broad benchmark helps many users compare methods, but each task still needs metrics that match its specific causal question.
936.dots: This paper sits directly inside the repo's causal-inference family, where many papers ask how to avoid being right for the wrong reason. Neighboring causal papers separate stable user preference from popularity, real fault causes from trace coincidences, and genuine graph pathways from misleading links. CausalBench addresses the shared infrastructure problem underneath those efforts: if every paper invents its own test, the field cannot learn which causal moves survive outside one narrow setting. It also connects to fairness and responsible evaluation, because the abstract explicitly names fairness, bias awareness, scientific objectivity, and reproducibility. It connects to systems work as well, since hardware and software platforms can change measured performance. Unlike a method paper that proposes one way to estimate a cause, this workshop tries to improve the map by which causal methods are selected, compared, and trusted.
936.ww: The effort should help because it attacks a hidden source of confusion before users make decisions. A causal model is already trying to control for false explanations inside data. If the evaluation of that model is itself uncontrolled, the field recreates the same problem one level higher: a reported win may be caused by dataset choice, metric choice, platform choice, or missing task coverage rather than by a better causal method. Shared, public, configurable benchmarks reduce that ambiguity. Public availability lets other groups repeat the test. Shared metrics make scores comparable. Configurability lets users see when a method is sensitive to data or platform conditions instead of treating one result as universal. Categorizing benchmarks into meaningful groups also prevents unfair comparisons between unlike tasks. A method for drawing causal structure should not be judged as if it were mainly estimating a treatment effect, and a metric for one failure may miss another. The workshop works by making the terms of comparison explicit, so disagreement can move from vague claims to checkable test design.
936.po: The payoff is better model selection and more objective progress in causal learning. According to the abstract, users currently struggle to choose the right setup for a specific problem because model performance changes across data and platforms. A unified, public, configurable benchmarking effort would give researchers common ground for comparing available solutions and designing new algorithms. It would also make gaps visible: missing datasets, weak metrics, poorly covered tasks, or bias risks that need attention. The practical gain is not one winning model, but a cleaner way to decide what evidence supports a causal model's claimed usefulness.
936.limits: The abstract describes a workshop call and research agenda, not a completed benchmark with reported results. Its value depends on whether the community actually contributes high-quality datasets, metrics, and reproducible evaluation protocols. A unified benchmark can also create false confidence if users treat its tasks as the whole field; real causal problems may contain hidden variables, policy constraints, or domain details absent from public tests. Hardware and software variation can be measured only if the benchmark records it carefully. Finally, the provided abstract is truncated, so the exact topics, submission scope, and concrete benchmark design are not fully visible here.

937.bp: Academic search is the plumbing behind many research decisions. A scholar needs papers to read, an author needs papers to cite, and a program committee or funding agency needs reviewers who understand a submission and will judge it fairly. Those are not separate chores in practice. They all ask the same question: from a huge and changing scholarly record, which papers or people are closest to this need? Scholar API, or SAPI, serves that shared problem by making academic search and recommendation pieces easier to combine. The paper is not mainly presenting one ranking model as the final answer. It treats academic search as an ecosystem where many groups may build partial tools: one source may have better citation data, another may have useful paper descriptions, another may supply a different way to measure scholarly closeness. SAPI tries to provide a simple access layer, data infrastructure, and federation mechanism so these pieces can be mashed up rather than rebuilt in isolation.
937.wh: The difficulty starts with the size and shape of scholarship. A paper is not only a title and abstract. It lives in a citation graph, belongs to topical neighborhoods, may be relevant for reading, citing, reviewing, or funding, and may be described differently by different services. A simple search box can miss useful papers because authors use different words for related ideas. A single recommendation engine can be too narrow because academic search has many users and many goals. Reviewer assignment is especially delicate: the system must find people who are well informed and sympathetic to the topic area, not merely people whose names share words with the submission. The abstract also points to a coordination problem. Many parties can offer partial solutions, but partial tools are less useful when every tool requires a separate data format, service contract, or local copy of the scholarly world. The hard part is therefore not only ranking papers; it is making diverse evidence sources comparable and reachable.
937.naive: A smart beginner would build one academic search service with one paper database, one similarity model, and one recommendation rule. For reading, it might return papers whose abstracts share words with a query. For citation help, it might return papers that cite or are cited by nearby papers. For reviewer assignment, it might match submission words to reviewer publications. That works for easy cases, but it breaks when different tasks need different evidence. A citation candidate, a reading recommendation, and a reviewer match are related but not identical. One local service may also miss useful sources maintained elsewhere. If every new method must be hand-wired into a separate system, creative combinations become expensive, and the field gets many isolated partial answers.
937.ap: The paper's central move is to make academic search composable. Instead of forcing everyone to choose one source and one representation of scholarly meaning, SAPI offers an easy API for combining solutions from different sources. In plain terms, it acts like a shared counter where tools can ask for papers, compare them using several available paper fingerprints, and combine outside services without each builder having to assemble the whole infrastructure again. The abstract names a federation mechanism, meaning SAPI can conveniently reach many sources rather than treating one local store as the only truth. It also exposes four selectable embeddings: Specter, ProNE-s, SciNCL, and a GNN. An embedding is a compact list of numbers used as a searchable fingerprint; papers judged related should receive fingerprints that sit near each other. SAPI's concrete contribution is to put several such fingerprints and service sources behind a flexible architecture, then demonstrate utility through a baseline implementation.
937.mech: The mechanism begins with academic objects and academic tasks. The objects are papers and, by implication, the citation relationships among papers and the external services that know about them. The tasks include recommending papers to read, finding papers to cite, and assigning submissions to suitable reviewers. SAPI first depends on an underlying data infrastructure that keeps these objects accessible in a common way. Rather than making a developer fetch and normalize every source manually, the API presents convenient access to many different sources through federation. Federation means the system can bring together answers or evidence from multiple services while hiding some of the connection work behind one interface. Next, a user or developer can choose among four paper fingerprints. Specter, SciNCL, and the GNN are described as deep neural methods based on BERT encodings of abstracts, fine-tuned using nearby documents in the citation graph. In plain language, they read abstract text into numeric descriptions and adjust those descriptions so citation neighbors count as meaningful context. ProNE-s is different: it uses spectral clustering of the citation graph, a linear-algebra method that studies link patterns directly. Once the chosen fingerprint is available, SAPI can compare papers by closeness, retrieve nearby candidates, or feed those candidates into a recommendation or reviewer-matching baseline. The output is not one fixed academic-search product, but a reusable API path for building such products from shared sources and selectable representations.
937.math: The main mathematical ideas are similarity, graph structure, linear algebra, and ranking or matching. Similarity means replacing the vague phrase related paper with a measurable comparison. Each paper receives a compact numeric fingerprint, and two papers whose fingerprints are close are treated as more likely to be useful neighbors. This is powerful because search, citation recommendation, and reviewer assignment all need a small useful set from a huge scholarly pile. The risk is compression: a paper's full meaning, method, venue, and audience are squeezed into numbers, so some detail is lost. The graph idea comes from citations. Papers are nodes, citation relationships are links, and nearby nodes carry evidence because authors often cite work that is intellectually related. Neural methods named in the abstract combine abstract text with citation-neighbor training, which means the model is rewarded when text descriptions and citation neighborhoods agree. ProNE-s uses spectral clustering, which is linear algebra over the citation graph: it looks for large-scale link patterns by studying how the graph can be decomposed into smooth directions or communities. Ranking then orders candidate papers, while reviewer assignment becomes matching: pairing a submission with people whose publication neighborhoods and topics fit. The tradeoff is flexibility versus trust. Multiple fingerprints let builders choose the comparison language, but the chosen math is only useful if nearness reflects the real scholarly decision.
937.dots: In the repo's family map, this paper sits between information retrieval, recommendation, similarity, matching, and graph reasoning. It is an information-retrieval paper because it asks how to find a small useful set of scholarly objects from a very large collection. It is a recommender-systems paper because reading suggestions and citation suggestions are choices made under partial evidence about what a researcher needs next. It is also a matching paper because reviewer assignment is not just finding a nearby paper; it pairs scarce expert attention with submissions. The similarity concept is central because SAPI exposes several numeric paper fingerprints whose closeness can drive search. The graph concept enters through citations, where links between papers are treated as evidence that scholarly ideas are related. Neighboring repo examples such as CiteLLM use retrieval and paragraph-level similarity for citation support, while broader retrieval-augmented and fact-checking papers ask how fetched evidence should support downstream decisions. SAPI's distinctive role is infrastructural: it tries to make those kinds of experiments easier to combine across sources.
937.ww: The approach should help because academic-search quality often depends on combining evidence that no single source or representation captures alone. Abstract text is useful because it says what a paper claims to be about, but wording varies across fields and authors. Citations are useful because they reveal scholarly relationships created by authors, but citation links can reflect visibility, fashion, or missing coverage as well as topic. Neural paper fingerprints can blend wording with citation-neighborhood signals, while ProNE-s gives a graph-only linear-algebra alternative. By exposing several choices through one API, SAPI lets a builder test or combine comparison languages instead of betting the whole application on one. The federation mechanism helps for a different reason: academic search has many partial providers, and creative tools often fail at the plumbing stage before their ranking idea can be tried.
